newsitem.title: UK: POLL-Summit seen boosting EMU launch chances.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Summit seen boosting EMU launch chances.

text.p: Experts predict that European economic and monetary union (EMU) stands an average 83 percent chance of starting on time, compared with a 79 percent likelihood a month ago, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.
The monthly survey of 33 economists, think tanks and political analysts across Europe showed that expectations were high that the euro would have a broad membership at its launch.

Analysts in the poll, conducted between August 6 and 8, said they believed the results of the Amsterdam summit, where European Union (EU) states reaffirmed their commitment to the euro, had contributed to the bullish mood.

"Expectations are growing as a consequence of the Amsterdam summit, the euro coin has been presented and the comments by EU leaders have reaffirmed the time schedule," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
He said the political will to launch euro on time was outweighing the necessity for aspiring members to meet strict economic targets.
"The whole process is determined by political movements," he added.
Caroline Newhouse-Cohen, economist with Louis Dreyfus Finance in Paris, agreed.
"The political will of all the European governments has never been so strong," she said.

As in the July poll, all respondents predicted that the EMU heavyweights, the core group of Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, would be sure favourites to meet the 1999 deadline.
The survey also showed strong support for the likelihood of first-wave membership for Finland, Ireland, Spain and Portugal.
Ninety-seven percent and 94 percent of contributors saw Ireland and Finland respectively as founder members, while Portugal and Spain each received the support of 91 percent of the respondents.
"Ireland's (budget deficit-to-GDP) ratio has year after year decreased at a substantial pace...They will certainly be in the first round of monetary union," said Newhouse-Cohen.
"For Finland...progress can be read in their figures and they have a good chance to fulfil the full criteria."
More analysts opted for Italy's first-wave entry this month -- 64 percent compared with July's 54 percent.

"We give Italy more than half a chance of joining because the criteria will be relaxed for France and they will have to do the same for Italy," said Raents Abma, economist at the VNO-VCW employers' confederation in the Netherlands.
Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Greece were again the EMU underdogs of Europe, with few or no contributors giving those countries any chance of founder membership.
